title: Ruth Gleans in Boaz's Field
overview: Ruth Chapter 2 narrates the providential care and kindness extended to Ruth, a Moabitess widow, as she gleans in the fields of Boaz, a wealthy kinsman of Naomi’s late husband. This chapter highlights themes of divine provision, loyalty, and redemption, illustrating how God’s hand is at work through human kindness and faithfulness. Ruth’s humble obedience and Boaz’s generosity set the stage for the unfolding redemption story central to the book. The chapter also deepens the relationship between Ruth and Naomi, emphasizing trust in God’s provision amid hardship. It serves as a key turning point in the narrative, demonstrating God’s faithfulness to those who seek refuge under His wings.
structure:
**Verses 1-3: Introduction of Boaz and Ruth’s Initiative.** Naomi’s relative Boaz is introduced as a wealthy and influential man, and Ruth takes the initiative to glean in his fields, seeking favor and sustenance.

**Verses 4-7: Boaz’s Kindness Recognized.** Boaz arrives, blesses his workers, and inquires about Ruth. The servant explains her situation, highlighting her loyalty to Naomi and her diligence in gleaning.

**Verses 8-16: Boaz’s Protection and Provision for Ruth.** Boaz personally instructs Ruth to stay close to his maidens for safety and provision, commands his servants to protect her, and ensures she has enough food and opportunity to glean freely.

**Verses 17-23: Ruth’s Return and Naomi’s Blessing.** Ruth returns with a substantial amount of grain, shares it with Naomi, and Naomi blesses Boaz for his kindness. Ruth continues to glean in Boaz’s fields until the harvest ends, demonstrating ongoing provision and protection.

keyVerses.text: The LORD recompense thy work, and a full reward be given thee of the LORD God of Israel, under whose wings thou art come to trust.
keyVerses.significance: This verse encapsulates the theme of divine protection and blessing. Boaz’s blessing acknowledges Ruth’s faith and trust in God, portraying God as a refuge and rewarder of faithful service, which is central to the chapter’s message of providence.

keyVerses.text: Then said Boaz unto Ruth, Hearest thou not, my daughter? Go not to glean in another field, neither go from hence, but abide here fast by my maidens:
keyVerses.significance: Boaz’s protective command reveals his kindness and care, symbolizing God’s provision and protection for the vulnerable. It also foreshadows Boaz’s role as a kinsman-redeemer, emphasizing security and favor.

keyVerses.text: And Boaz answered and said unto her, It hath fully been shewed me, all that thou hast done unto thy mother in law since the death of thine husband: and how thou hast left thy father and thy mother, and the land of thy nativity, and art come unto a people which thou knewest not heretofore .
keyVerses.significance: Boaz’s recognition of Ruth’s loyalty and sacrifice highlights her faithfulness and courage. This acknowledgment underscores the theme of covenant loyalty and God’s providential guidance in her life.

keyVerses.text: And Boaz said unto her, At mealtime come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar. And she sat beside the reapers: and he reached her parched corn, and she did eat, and was sufficed, and left.
keyVerses.significance: This verse illustrates Boaz’s generosity and hospitality, reflecting God’s abundant provision. It also shows Ruth’s acceptance into the community, symbolizing inclusion and blessing.

characters.name: Ruth
characters.description: A Moabitess widow who demonstrates loyalty to Naomi and faith in God by gleaning in the fields. Her humility, diligence, and trust in God’s provision are central to the chapter’s narrative.

characters.name: Boaz
characters.description: A wealthy and honorable kinsman of Naomi’s late husband. He shows kindness, protection, and generosity to Ruth, acting as a figure of God’s providence and foreshadowing his role as redeemer.

characters.name: Naomi
characters.description: Ruth’s mother-in-law who guides and encourages Ruth to glean in Boaz’s fields. She recognizes God’s hand in Boaz’s kindness and expresses hope in his role as a kinsman-redeemer.

themes.description: God’s unseen hand is evident in Ruth’s chance to glean in Boaz’s field and in Boaz’s kindness. This chapter shows how God provides for His people through human agents and circumstances.
Ruth’s steadfast loyalty to Naomi and her faithfulness in obedience highlight covenantal faithfulness, a key biblical theme that God honors and blesses.
Boaz’s protection of Ruth and his generosity foreshadow the redemptive role he will play. This theme connects to the broader biblical narrative of God as redeemer and protector of the vulnerable.

historicalContext: Ruth is set during the period of the Judges (circa 1200-1050 BC), a time of social and political instability in Israel. The story takes place in Bethlehem, a small town in Judah, where agricultural practices such as gleaning were legally mandated to provide for the poor and foreigners (Leviticus 19:9-10). The custom of gleaning allowed widows and the marginalized to gather leftover crops after harvesters, reflecting God’s provision for the needy. The concept of a kinsman-redeemer, a relative who could redeem property or marry a widow to preserve family lineage, was a vital social institution in Israelite culture. Understanding these customs is essential to grasp the significance of Boaz’s actions and Ruth’s situation.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God’s sovereign providence in orchestrating events for His glory. Ruth’s gleaning in Boaz’s field is seen as a clear example of God’s providential care for His elect, rewarding faithfulness and obedience.
Dispensationalists highlight the literal fulfillment of the kinsman-redeemer role in Boaz, viewing this chapter as a type pointing forward to Christ’s ultimate redemption of His people.

Early Church Fathers often interpreted Boaz as a Christ figure, with Ruth representing the Gentile believer coming under God’s protective wings, emphasizing the inclusion of Gentiles into God’s covenant family.

crossReferences.connection: Establishes the law of leaving gleanings for the poor and foreigners, which Ruth follows in this chapter.
Describes the levirate marriage and kinsman-redeemer concept that Boaz embodies.
The imagery of God’s protective wings parallels Boaz’s blessing of Ruth under God’s wings.
Ruth is mentioned in the genealogy of Christ, linking this chapter’s events to the Messianic lineage.
God’s promise of protection and strength resonates with Boaz’s protective care for Ruth.

application: Trust God’s providence even in difficult circumstances, knowing He can provide through unexpected means.
Demonstrate loyalty and faithfulness in relationships, reflecting God’s covenantal love.
Show kindness and protection to those in need, modeling Boaz’s generosity.
Seek refuge under God’s wings through faith, trusting His care and protection.
Be diligent and humble in service, as Ruth was in her gleaning.
Encourage and support others who are vulnerable, just as Naomi guided Ruth.
conclusion: Ruth Chapter 2 powerfully illustrates God’s providential care through the kindness of Boaz and the faithfulness of Ruth. It teaches believers to trust in God’s provision, to act with loyalty and generosity, and to recognize God’s protective hand in everyday circumstances. This chapter not only advances the redemption narrative but also offers timeless lessons on faith, obedience, and God’s faithful provision for His people.
timeline: Circa 1200-1050 BC - Period of the Judges in Israel

definitions.definition: To gather leftover grain or produce from the fields after the main harvest, a practice commanded by God to provide for the poor and foreigners.
A relative who has legal and familial responsibilities, especially in matters of redemption and protection of family inheritance.
A close relative who has the duty to redeem a family member in trouble, such as marrying a widow to preserve the family line or redeeming property.

definitions.term: Under whose wings thou art come to trust
definitions.definition: A metaphor describing seeking refuge and protection under God’s care, likened to a bird sheltering its young.
A female from Moab, a neighboring nation often viewed as outside the covenant community, highlighting Ruth’s status as a foreigner.

outline.heading: Introduction of Boaz and Ruth’s Gleaning
outline.description: Naomi’s kinsman Boaz is introduced, and Ruth takes initiative to glean in his fields, seeking provision and favor.

outline.heading: Boaz’s Arrival and Inquiry
outline.description: Boaz blesses his workers and inquires about Ruth, learning of her loyalty and diligence from his servant.

outline.heading: Boaz’s Protection and Provision
outline.description: Boaz commands Ruth to stay near his maidens for safety, instructs his servants to protect her, and provides food and opportunity for her to glean abundantly.

outline.heading: Ruth’s Return and Naomi’s Blessing
outline.description: Ruth returns with a generous harvest, shares with Naomi, who blesses Boaz. Ruth continues gleaning until the harvest ends, showing ongoing provision.
